demo-1-play-a-registry-from-creation-to-.text: Demo 1: play a registry from creation to termination.

As a Cardano developer who knows wallets, faucets and Koios but has never used Singular, you want to watch a registry work before you read how it is built: a registry is created, a key is put in it, changed and ended, the registry refuses what it must refuse, and two people sign their writes in two different ways. Demo 1 introduces that play. The steps, and the programs to run them, live in a repository of their own, singular-demo. This page says what the play shows and where to play it.

what-the-play-shows.text: Two people, Alice and Bob, share one registry. Its application, open datum, lets a key carry a payload that only the key's controller may replace, and keeps the protected deposit with the live holding. Booking permanent termination donates that deposit to the treasury.

A registration starts as a pending request. Any wallet may fold it, making the key active and delivering its token, payload and protected deposit to the committed holding. Its controller may update the payload without spending the registry state.

The controller books permanent termination by donating the protected deposit to the treasury and moving the active token into a pending termination request. Any wallet may fold that request, burning its approval and active token and making the key permanently terminal. The folder receives the request's held value and pays the transaction fee. A termination has no reclaim window.

A registration that nobody folds can be reclaimed by its refund address inside its reclaim window. After that window, anyone can clean it up: the protected deposit returns to the refund address and the caller receives the held value above that deposit. A reclaim outside its window and a cleanup before its window are refused. The command guide gives the flags and receipts for each operation.

The two people sign in the two ways Singular offers. Alice names her vault, a file holding her signing key sealed by a passphrase, and one command builds, signs and sends. Bob names only his wallet's address and a bundle file: the command builds the transactions into the file, signs nothing, and exits with status 19, which means it is waiting for signatures. Then Bob signs the bundle from his vault and sends it, so the machine that builds a write never needs to hold the key.

where-to-play-it.text: The demo repository records its release and the steps it supports. The table lists five entry points: the recorded run to watch, the Killercoda scenario to play in a browser, the step-by-step page to paste from, which needs the programs, and the Nix shell and the Ubuntu kit, which are two ways to get the programs. To play on your own machine, start with the step-by-step page.
The singular-demo repository describes the shell and the kit, what each is pinned to and what it was tested on.

what-it-does-not-claim.text: Everything the step-by-step page runs happens on a private test chain that it starts; nothing touches a public network. The open datum application protects the payload and the deposit and nothing more: it demonstrates the registry's mechanics. The receipts of a play are evidence of behaviour on a private chain only, and no complete conformance is claimed here. What the project does claim, and what it leaves open, is on the conformance evidence page. What is deployed on the public preprod network, and the transactions the project's own journeys submitted there, are recorded in the preprod record.

the-release-behind-it.text: The play runs a release of Singular. These pages are about the release itself, not about the steps: install the commands without Nix and download and verify a release.
